state: Seven current registered canonical objects. Five owners and eleven available short-summary entries updated at named endpoint source scope; no new owners or blanket recertification of retained clinical assertions.

records.name: Kaplan-Meier curve, censoring and proportional hazards
records.tldr: A Kaplan-Meier curve estimates a group's probability of remaining alive or free of a specified event from a stated time origin. Events make steps; censoring ends observation without an event and changes later risk sets. It is not an individual forecast.
records.summary:
Survival endpoints are awkward because at the moment of analysis most patients have not died or progressed and have been followed for different lengths of time. The Kaplan-Meier method handles this by working through time step by step: at each event it multiplies the survival probability so far by the fraction of patients still at risk who survived that moment. Patients who are alive at their last visit are censored, meaning they contribute follow-up up to that point and then drop out of the calculation without being counted as an event. The result is the stepped curve in every trial paper, with a number-at-risk table underneath showing how many patients remain at each time; when that number gets small, the tail of the curve is unreliable however dramatic it looks. The median survival is where the curve crosses 50 percent, and a fixed-time estimate such as five-year survival is read off at that time.

The log-rank test compares survival distributions. The usual constant-effect Cox model assumes proportional hazards, meaning a constant hazard ratio over time. The Kaplan-Meier calculation itself does not impose a constant between-group hazard ratio. Nonproportional hazards can reduce the power of a log-rank comparison and make a single hazard ratio an incomplete account of treatment effect. A prespecified restricted mean survival-time contrast describes the difference in areas under the curves up to a stated horizon; a fixed-time survival contrast answers another question. Neither a late plateau nor a group hazard ratio predicts one individual's future.

Censoring hides a trap. The method assumes patients censored at a given time are no more or less likely to have the event than those still being followed. If patients leave a trial because they are doing badly, or are censored when they start another therapy, the curve is biased upwards. Informative censoring is one reason progression-free survival read from investigator scans can flatter an open-label trial, and one reason the estimand framework asks trialists to say in advance how they will treat patients who switch, stop or are lost.

notes: A Kaplan-Meier curve estimates the probability of remaining free of a defined event from a stated starting time while accounting for incomplete follow-up. At each event time, the previous estimate is multiplied by the fraction of people still at risk just before that time who avoid the event. Right censoring means observation ended without the event being seen, for example at cutoff or loss to follow-up. It leaves the current height unchanged but removes that person from later risk sets. A censor tick is neither an event nor proof of permanent event freedom. Interpretation requires censoring to be sufficiently independent of future event time within the analysis; losing contact because disease is worsening can bias the estimate.

Five fictional participants start follow-up for first recurrence, with no deaths in this example. One recurrence at month 1 leaves 4/5, or 80%, recurrence-free. One person is censored at month 2, so the estimate remains 80% but only three are at risk before the next recurrence at month 3. The new estimate is (4/5) × (2/3) = 8/15, about 53.3%. Subtracting two observed recurrences from the original five would ignore the missing later observation. The censored person is known to have been recurrence-free only through month 2; the group estimate does not fill in that person's month-3 outcome. The example stops at month 3 and supplies no later outcome, confidence interval or individual prognosis.

A five-year curve height is an estimate from its stated origin. A landmark analysis instead selects people meeting a condition at a later time, such as being observed and event-free at month 6, then evaluates subsequent outcomes. It changes the population and clock and handles early events differently from the original trial comparison. Classifying people by a later response can also bias survival comparisons if timing is mishandled. Read the endpoint, origin, cutoff, censoring rules, confidence intervals and number-at-risk table together. At-risk counts are changing denominators, not new enrolment; a flat late tail may rest on very few people and does not establish cure. Median survival is when the curve reaches 50%; “not reached” means it did not reach that level during observed follow-up. Median follow-up describes observation time. Neither statement implies there were no events. Curve height is not a hazard ratio, and curve separation needs a suitable study design for a causal interpretation.

Treating deaths that occur before the recurrence of interest as censoring and calculating one minus Kaplan-Meier targets a different quantity from cumulative incidence and can overstate that real-world recurrence probability. Cumulative incidence addresses that competing-risk question. The nonparametric Aalen-Johansen estimator estimates state probabilities, including cumulative incidence as a competing-risk special case, under the relevant event, observation and censoring assumptions. Fine-Gray regression is a separate model for covariate effects on the subdistribution hazard. Austin and colleagues' 2016 tutorial supports the bias and hazard distinctions; Therneau, Crowson and Atkinson's September 2026 technical vignette separately supplies the Aalen-Johansen method name and its relationship to cumulative incidence. Neither estimator removes the need for an appropriate event definition and follow-up.

The Kaplan-Meier event-fraction calculation does not specify a constant between-group hazard ratio. In Royston and Parmar's 2013 simulations, log-rank significance levels remained close to their planned value under the studied proportional and nonproportional patterns, while power differed. That illustrates why a model assumption, a test's calibration and its power are separate questions; it is not proof that every survival analysis is valid.

records.name: Event-free / disease-free survival (EFS, DFS, iDFS, RFS)
records.tldr: In early-stage cancer: how long patients stay free of recurrence, progression, or death.
records.summary: Event-free survival and its relatives, disease-free survival, invasive disease-free survival and recurrence-free survival, are the endpoints used in early-stage cancer to measure how long patients stay free of recurrence, progression or death. Event definitions differ by trial: EFS in KEYNOTE-522 counts progression that precludes surgery, iDFS in monarchE and NATALEE counts invasive recurrence, second cancers and death, and RFS is the measure in INTerpath-001 (V940-001). Use of an endpoint to support a particular approval does not make every endpoint with that name a validated substitute for overall survival. FDA guidance distinguishes direct clinical benefit, established surrogate evidence and the less established surrogate evidence that can support accelerated approval, with confirmatory obligations. They appear in the NADINA, KEYNOTE-716, KEYNOTE-689, MATTERHORN, ZUMA-7, ASCENT-05 / OptimICE-RD and TROPION-Breast03 trial records, in the Neuroblastoma (paediatric) entry and in the KEYNOTE-522 and CheckMate 816 papers.

notes: Disease-free survival is the primary endpoint of the adjuvant pancreatic cancer trials: in PRODIGE 24 median disease-free survival was 21.6 months with modified FOLFIRINOX against 12.8 months with gemcitabine (hazard ratio 0.58 for a cancer-related event, second cancer or death), and overall survival followed (Conroy 2018). The definition, time from randomisation to any event irrespective of cause, follows the adjuvant-trial consensus (Punt 2007).

A survival endpoint defines when the clock starts and which outcomes stop it, usually at the first qualifying event. Overall survival counts death from any cause. Event-free survival uses its protocol's prespecified event set; a neoadjuvant trial may include progression preventing definitive surgery, recurrence, a second primary cancer and death. Disease-free survival is also study-defined and cannot automatically be exchanged for event-free or invasive disease-free survival. Progression-free survival usually counts objective progression or death, with scan criteria, assessment times and missing-assessment rules attached. Participant dates, event types, follow-up status, censoring and cutoff determine the resulting curve, time-specific estimate or rate comparison and its uncertainty. An acronym or a second operation alone does not establish which events count. FDA's December 2018 nonbinding guidance discusses evidence by indication and pathway. It describes progression-free survival as able, depending on disease, context and effect size, to support accelerated approval, support traditional approval or represent direct clinical benefit. This does not universally validate it as a substitute for overall survival. A favourable distant-event endpoint does not settle local control or overall survival. An endpoint association also differs from proof that acting on a biomarker improves outcomes.

In the event table reproduced by STEEP 2.0 in 2021, invasive disease-free survival counts invasive local, regional, distant and contralateral breast events, a second nonbreast invasive primary, and death from any cause; in situ disease is excluded. STEEP 2.0 defines invasive breast cancer-free survival as a distinct endpoint excluding second nonbreast primaries, rather than silently removing them from invasive disease-free survival. Distant recurrence-free interval counts distant recurrence or breast-cancer death under STEEP, whereas its distant relapse-free survival row counts death from any cause. The paper's actual rules remain essential. A person alive after a local invasive recurrence with no distant recurrence can therefore have an invasive disease-free-survival event without an overall-survival or distant-recurrence-free-interval event. These rules are read from the 2021 table; the trial's own starting clock, first-event and competing-event rules still need checking.

The starting date may be randomisation, consent, surgery or biomarker assessment. KEYNOTE-522 used pathological complete response and event-free survival as co-primary endpoints; renaming its event-free-survival result invasive disease-free survival changes the claim. For a fictional participant with progression at month 12 and death at month 30, both measured from randomisation, progression-free survival stops at month 12 while overall survival continues to month 30. Those dates describe a known individual history, not censoring or a survival-probability estimate. A postoperative cohort or another endpoint requires its own origin and event rules.

Among 1,000 fictional participants, suppose 50 first recurrences are recorded and 20 are assigned to site X, with some follow-up incomplete. The calculation 20/50 = 40% describes the share of recorded first recurrences assigned to X. The calculation 20/1,000 = 2% describes a crude fraction of enrolled participants with that recorded event. Neither supplies five-year risk. Death before recurrence prevents recurrence, and another first site prevents X from being the first site; later recurrence at X is a different endpoint. A cumulative-incidence analysis can account for follow-up and competing events under its assumptions. The nonparametric Aalen-Johansen estimator supplies that estimate, while Fine-Gray regression models covariate effects on the subdistribution hazard. The method-name attribution comes from Therneau, Crowson and Atkinson's technical vignette, separately from Austin's competing-risk discussion. Turning the 40% site share into everyone's five-year risk changes both denominator and horizon without a supporting analysis.

STEEP 2.0's 2021 Table 1 specifies exclusions as well as event categories for adjuvant breast-cancer studies. Its second primary nonbreast cancer category excludes basal-cell and squamous-cell skin carcinomas and in situ carcinomas. Lobular carcinoma in situ is not counted as an event. These are the table's conventions; a study's actual endpoint definition and protocol remain part of its result.

records.name: Surrogate endpoint validation: which stand-ins have earned trust
records.tldr: A surrogate endpoint only deserves trust if trials have shown that moving it moves the outcome that matters, in that disease and for that kind of drug; some stand-ins have passed that test, several have not, and the record differs endpoint by endpoint.
records.summary:
A marker can be associated with a later outcome without being validated as a substitute for it. For treatment-effect surrogacy, the question is whether changes caused by treatment in the proposed surrogate predict changes in the outcome of interest. Trial-level validation examines treatment effects across suitable randomised studies, with attention to disease, treatment class, endpoint and intended outcome. A patient-level association alone cannot establish that relationship.

Named examples require their own population, regimen and analysis. In the final TROPION-Breast01 analysis of previously treated hormone-receptor-positive, HER2-negative advanced breast cancer, overall survival was not statistically significantly improved (hazard ratio 1.01, 95% confidence interval 0.83 to 1.22); this does not establish exactly zero effect. Later antibody-drug-conjugate use was imbalanced between arms (12.3% with datopotamab deruxtecan and 24.0% with chemotherapy); the authors note that it may have affected the survival result. DUO-O met its progression-free-survival endpoints for a specified multi-drug strategy in newly diagnosed non-BRCA-mutated advanced ovarian cancer, while the reported overall-survival analysis was interim at 39% maturity. BEAT-meso tested adding atezolizumab to bevacizumab and chemotherapy in advanced pleural mesothelioma: progression-free survival improved, while its primary overall-survival comparison did not meet statistical significance. These are distinct comparisons, rather than interchangeable evidence that progression-free survival cannot matter.

Olaratumab is not an example of approval resting on response rate alone. FDA's 2016 review described an uncertain survival estimate from a small randomised study as central to accelerated approval and did not regard its response-rate effect as clinically meaningful. ANNOUNCE subsequently did not confirm the survival benefit. Lurbinectedin's 2020 accelerated approval instead relied on response rate and duration of response. ATLANTIS tested lower-dose lurbinectedin combined with doxorubicin against chemotherapy in relapsed small-cell lung cancer; it did not demonstrate a statistically significant survival improvement. That result must retain its combination, dose and comparator rather than being described as a test of the approved monotherapy regimen.

For a trial that improves a surrogate, ask whether trial-level validation applies to this disease, treatment class and intended outcome. Read the clinical-outcome estimate and its uncertainty for benefit and harm compatible with the data, and check the status of any required confirmatory trial. A nonsignificant survival comparison alone establishes neither equivalence nor absence of harm.

Other linked records include CodeBreaK 200, adjuvant trials, residual-disease trials and UKCTOCS screening. They remain related studies, rather than interchangeable validation of a surrogate. This account does not reassert their previously listed outcome or regulatory-validation claims, which require source-specific verification. The linked trial-design bottleneck and proposal for independent surrogate validation extend the methodological questions.

notes: A surrogate is a measured outcome used in place of a direct clinical-benefit outcome, with evidence needed for that substitution in the intended setting. Two relationships must be separated: people with a favourable marker may have better outcomes, while treatments that improve that marker may or may not improve the outcome. The first is a prognostic association; the second concerns agreement between treatment effects across suitable randomised comparisons. A treatment can change another pathway, later disease or toxicity as well as the marker. Validation is specific to disease, treatment context and intended outcome. An early measure is not automatically validated, and regulatory acceptance in one programme does not transfer to another. “Validated” and “reasonably likely to predict benefit” carry different evidence claims. Even a pathology or imaging response does not capture every benefit and harm.

Imagine twenty fictional people grouped by whether they achieved pathological complete response, with complete event follow-up to three years. A difference in events between those groups would describe an association after response was achieved, rather than preserve a randomised treatment comparison. Across six fictional randomised trials, a different analysis would compare each trial's treatment-related gain in response with its gain in three-year event-free survival, both in percentage points. Those are different units of evidence; neither constructed example is the CTNeoBC dataset. Similarly, a fictional trial increasing complete response from 40/100 to 55/100 establishes a 15-percentage-point response difference under its definition, with uncertainty still needed. Immature survival follow-up does not supply a proven survival gain.

Pathological complete response is assessed in the surgical specimen after neoadjuvant treatment, rather than a presurgical scan or biopsy. Retain the exact definition, such as ypT0/Tis ypN0 meaning no invasive disease in breast or nodes, and how missing surgery or specimens affect denominators. CTNeoBC pooled 11,955 people from 12 trials: achieving that response was associated with event-free-survival HR 0.48 and overall-survival HR 0.36; corresponding triple-negative subgroup estimates were 0.24 and 0.16. Yet trial-level R-squared was 0.03 for event-free survival (95% interval 0.00 to 0.25) and 0.24 for overall survival (0.00 to 0.70). Conforti and colleagues' analysis of 54 trials and 32,611 participants found R-squared 0.14 (95% interval 0.00 to 0.29) for disease-free and 0.08 (0.00 to 0.22) for overall survival. R-squared here is the share of variation in the treatment effects on survival that is explained by the treatment effects on pathological complete response; 1 would be a perfect fit. Thus response can be strongly associated with outcomes among participants while remaining a weak substitute for treatment effects across trials. This fitted association is not an individually validated risk prediction. These fitted associations concern variation in treatment effects across trials, with substantial uncertainty; they are not personal prognosis models.

A weak trial-level association does not mean no regimen can improve both endpoints. KEYNOTE-522 reported a 13.6-percentage-point pathological-response gain and subsequently event-free and overall-survival gains, each in its own analysis. One regimen's success does not validate the surrogate across regimens. For every comparison, retain population, intervention, comparator, assessment time and response uncertainty, then separately the survival event definition, starting clock and follow-up. A response association and a demonstrated treatment benefit remain different claims.

A fictional two-level example separates people from trials. In the patient panel, all 20 people have complete follow-up to year 3: 10 achieved a pathological complete response and 10 did not. Two of the first 10 and six of the second 10 have an event by year 3. These are groups defined by an achieved response, not randomized groups, so the contrast alone does not show what causing a response would do. In a separate trial panel, six points represent randomized A-minus-B comparisons. Their pairs of differences in pathological complete response rate and 3-year event-free survival rate, both in percentage points, are (5, 6), (8, -3), (10, 2), (12, -6), (15, 4) and (18, 0). Each point is a treatment comparison rather than a person. The invented pairs supply no fitted coefficient, validated surrogate relationship or individual forecast and are not CTNeoBC observations.

records.name: Objective response rate (ORR)
records.tldr: Objective response rate is the proportion of a stated analysis population meeting complete or partial response criteria. It is not the percentage by which every tumour shrank.
records.summary:
Objective response rate, also called overall response rate, counts participants meeting the specified complete or partial response criteria. Stable disease is excluded. Keep the denominator, measurable-disease requirements, biomarker rules, assessment window, reviewer, confirmation, data cutoff and missing-data handling with the percentage and confidence interval. A lesion-level fraction has a different denominator from a participant-level rate.

Under RECIST 1.1, the target partial-response measurement uses a decline in selected diameters from baseline; overall response also considers non-target and new disease. A 30 percent ORR means that proportion met the response definition, rather than every tumour shrinking 30 percent or the total tumour volume falling by that amount. Best response over follow-up and status at a fixed visit are different measures.

Confirmed and unconfirmed rates must retain their definitions. RECIST requires confirmation in non-randomised response-primary trials, while other designs and protocols have their own stated rules. Response magnitude and duration can support regulatory decisions in a specified context; a response rate is not automatically comparative survival benefit or a personal forecast.

notes: DCR and CBR may add protocol-defined stable disease and minimum-duration conditions; adding those participants changes the endpoint rather than increasing ORR. Duration of response concerns the responding population and its own starting time.

Fictional response example: among 20 people with complete assessment, four partial responses and six additional stable-disease outcomes give an objective response rate of 4/20, or 20%, and a disease-control rate of 10/20, or 50%. A clinical-benefit rate that requires durable stable disease cannot be calculated until the duration rule and follow-up are supplied. These are participant-level outcomes, not a fraction of tumour cells killed. Response criteria, confirmation, assessment period, denominator and missing-result rules stay with the number; neither label alone establishes survival or quality-of-life benefit.

records.name: Duration of response (DoR) and disease control rate (DCR)
records.tldr: Duration describes how long a response lasts. Disease control and clinical benefit rates count protocol-defined categories and time windows, which need separate interpretation.
records.summary:
Duration of response describes time after an initial qualifying response in the responding population. RECIST 1.1 starts overall response duration when CR or PR is first documented and follows it to documented recurrence or progression. Duration of complete response has its own CR starting point. Neither clock is automatically the all-patient progression-free-survival clock.

Read the protocol’s handling of death, missed assessments, later treatment and censoring. Scan frequency and follow-up affect what can be observed. A median or an ongoing-response proportion describes the specified analysis; a median not yet reached does not mean responses will last forever.

Response rate and duration provide different information. Neither alone establishes an individual cure or a comparative survival advantage. FDA’s oncology endpoint guidance considers their meaning in the particular disease, treatment setting, available alternatives and benefit-risk context; duration does not automatically turn a survival curve into a plateau.

Disease control rate often includes complete response, partial response and qualifying stable disease. Clinical benefit rate can use a specified durable-stability rule. These names do not define one universal duration or prove symptom, quality-of-life or survival benefit. Stability in a single-arm study can partly reflect untreated disease behaviour. Response timing also depends on assessment schedules and the actual regimen, rather than a universal fast-versus-slow treatment-family rule.

notes: The 2013 bicalutamide study used a six-month CBR endpoint in its study-defined ER/PgR-negative, AR-positive advanced-breast population. The 2018 enzalutamide study used CBR at 16 weeks as primary and 24 weeks as secondary in advanced AR-expressing TNBC. These historical study definitions are examples, not current drug indications or universal eligibility rules.

The enzalutamide report analysed 118 enrolled participants and a 78-person evaluable subgroup. The latter required at least one post-baseline assessment and at least 10 percent nuclear AR staining, whereas entry used greater than zero AR staining. These are different populations; a subgroup rate must not silently replace the all-enrolled result.

In a separate fictional example, all 20 participants are assessed. Two have confirmed complete responses, four confirmed partial responses and eight stable disease at week 8. Three of those eight meet the example's prespecified 24-week stable-disease criterion. With 20 as the denominator, objective response is (2 + 4)/20 = 30%, disease control is (2 + 4 + 8)/20 = 70%, and the example's clinical benefit rate is (2 + 4 + 3)/20 = 45%. The 24-week requirement applies only to the stable-disease branch in this example. The other six participants' outcomes and the later outcomes of the five other participants with week-8 stable disease are not supplied. No additional response window, confidence interval, trajectory or survival result can be inferred from these aggregate counts. This is a different invented cohort from the response-rate example in the objective response rate record. These aggregate categories do not identify individual participants or supply their trajectories. Different protocols and analysis populations need not put objective response, disease control and clinical benefit rates into one universal ordering.

records.name: Complete response (CR) and partial response (PR)
records.tldr: Complete and partial responses are categories under specified assessment rules. Their definitions, confirmation and clinical meaning depend on the disease and study.
records.summary:
Complete response means that the assessment meets its specified criteria for no detectable tumour. The method, disease, body sites and time matter. It does not establish that every unseen cancer cell is absent or that the response will last.

RECIST 1.1 combines target, non-target and new-lesion findings. Target disappearance alone is not sufficient for overall complete response; pathological lymph nodes must meet the short-axis rule. Confirmation is required in non-randomised trials with response as the primary endpoint, rather than in every study. Report confirmed and unconfirmed results using the actual protocol.

An imaging category is different from a pathological response based on examined tissue. The exact pathological definition, including the tissue and any nodal requirements, must be stated. Response classification, symptom relief, duration and survival answer different questions.

Under RECIST 1.1, target-lesion partial response requires at least a 30 percent decline in the baseline sum of specified diameters, with the other disease findings considered for the overall category. This is not a 30 percent volume rule or a definition for every blood cancer. Disease-specific systems have their own criteria.

notes: A complete or partial response can inform a treatment study without independently proving a comparative survival benefit. FDA endpoint interpretation also depends on disease, setting, magnitude, durability, alternatives and benefit-risk context.

records.name: Stable disease
records.tldr: Stable disease means the assessment meets neither the response nor the progression criteria. It can include size changes and does not, by itself, show that treatment caused the stability.
records.summary:
Under RECIST 1.1, stable disease for target lesions means neither sufficient shrinkage for partial response nor sufficient increase for progression. Partial response requires at least a 30% fall in the sum of target-lesion diameters from baseline. Progression requires at least a 20% rise from the smallest sum recorded on study, including baseline if that was the smallest, together with an absolute increase of at least 5 mm. These rules use different reference measurements; stable disease is not simply a fixed band around baseline.

An overall assessment also checks non-target disease and new tumour lesions. Unequivocal non-target progression or an unequivocal new tumour lesion can mean progression despite stable target-lesion measurements. The study protocol sets assessment timing and any minimum interval for counting stability. Stable disease can include growth or shrinkage and does not show by itself that treatment caused the stability. FDA's December 2018 nonbinding endpoint guidance notes that stable disease in a single-arm trial may reflect the cancer's natural history. Its duration, symptoms, quality of life and comparative treatment effects are separate questions.

records.name: Partial response
records.tldr: The tumours have shrunk substantially (by at least 30% in total diameter) but not disappeared. Together with complete responses it makes up a trial's response rate.
records.summary:
Partial response is an assessment category rather than a measure of tumour volume. Under RECIST 1.1, target-lesion partial response requires at least a 30% decrease in the sum of specified diameters from baseline. The overall assessment also considers non-target disease and new tumour lesions; target shrinkage alone does not establish the overall category.

RECIST 1.1 requires confirmation in nonrandomized trials where response is the primary endpoint, rather than in every study. Keep the actual protocol, assessment timing and confirmed or unconfirmed status with the result. An objective response rate counts participants meeting complete or partial response criteria in a stated analysis population. Response magnitude and duration can inform regulatory decisions in a specified disease and treatment setting, but a response rate alone does not establish comparative survival or quality-of-life benefit. FDA's December 2018 endpoint guidance is nonbinding and discusses these context-specific distinctions.
